title: Needle-Valley latency-cost vignette
content:
One-pager sketch: Needle vs Valley burst shapes and their p50/p90/p99 impact on per-query $ and token-latency

Context
- We get frequent questions from SRE/product about why short high-intensity bursts ("needles") often cost more per-successful-query than longer, lower-intensity bursts ("valleys") even when aggregate token volume is similar. This is a quick analysis draft to accompany the platform playbook.

Objective
- Compare three synthetic session shapes and show: latency percentiles (p50/p90/p99), short-term slot utilization, KV cache hit influence, and amortized $/query under current Dedicated profile (g5x2-type equivalent).
- Produce simple ASCII charts that can be pasted into Slack/Confluence for non-graph consumers.

Measurement setup (short) - Workload generator: local harness (bench-v2) using replayed session lengths (sampled from production sessionizer, filtered to chatbot-intent).
- Model: open-Llama-13B-ish quantized (q4_0) baseline used for parity across runs.
- Hardware: dedicated pod with 2xA100 equivalent; slot packing enabled; KV caching ON/OFF toggles.
- Key metrics recorded: tokens generated, tail latency ms, slot occupancy %, tokens-per-slot, cost per-minute ($/min).
- Notes: bursts simulated as fixed-arrival Poisson within burst window; background steady traffic kept at 5% of capacity to mimic real background noise.

Session shapes (definitions)
1) Needle: 20 sessions arriving in 1s window, each 8 tokens avg generation (short requests)
2) Valley: 20 sessions arriving uniformly over 20s, each 8 tokens avg generation
3) Hybrid: 20 sessions in 5s window, variable lengths (half short, half medium 40 tokens)

Raw summary table (aggregated, synthetic)
- All runs normalized to same total tokens (~1600 tokens), same model, same allocation. Cost figures are hypothetical but consistent relative to each other.

Shape | p50(ms) | p90(ms) | p99(ms) | slot occ (%) | tokens/slot | $/query
Needle | 18 | 120 | 430 | 92 | 4.2 | 0.0048
Valley  | 16 |  40 | 110 | 38 | 12.4| 0.0032
Hybrid  | 17 |  78 | 220 | 66 | 7.3 | 0.0039

Quick interpretation
- Needle shows low median (lots of short responses) but severe tail amplification (p99 much higher) due to slot contention and frequent context-switch overheads; tokens/slot low -> poorer utilization -> higher $/query.
- Valley achieves better slot packing, higher tokens/slot and thus better amortization of fixed kernel and dispatch costs. Tail is much tamer.
- Hybrid sits between: when some medium-length sessions interleave, packing improves but tail still visible.

ASCII visual: occupancy timeline (0-20s) for one simulated run (Needle vs Valley) - Time axis: 0.........5.........10........15........20s
Needle:  |||||||||||||||||||||||||||||||||||||||||||||||||| (dense cluster 0-1s)
Valley :  |__|__|__|__|__|__|__|__|__|__|__|__|__|__|__|__|__|__|__| (spread)

p90 vs $/query scatter (per-shape mocked points)
- p90(ms) : $/query
  - Needle: 120ms : $0.0048  (★ high-tail tax)
  - Valley: 40ms  : $0.0032  (lower cost, lower tail)
  - Hybrid: 78ms : $0.0039

Small microtable: breakdown of overhead sources (percent of price delta Needle vs Valley)
- Cold-start/context-switch: 42%
- Slot fragmentation (low tokens/slot): 28%
- Kernel / memory thrash: 17%
- Network serialization & small-payload inefficiency: 13%

Developer notes / actionable knobs
- Prefetch batching: for Needle-like short bursts, increase opportunistic small-batch windows (20-50ms) to aggregate short requests; sim shows potential 15-25% reduction in $/query but slight p50 increase.
- KV cache steering: mark longer-sessions as high-prefetch candidates; eviction tuned to favor multi-turn sessions reduces Valley->Needle gap.
- Admission control: soft queueing (delay 30-80ms) reduces tail p99 at cost of p50 for some SLA classes.
- Model stitching: for micro-needles, route to smaller model variants for immediate tokens then stitch heavier model for longer turns. Could yield 20-45% $/query savings in needle regime.

Questions / unresolved
- How representative are our synthetic burst arrival assumptions vs actual product microbursts (need deeper sampling across customers)? TODO: pull 7-day session arrival histograms. (JIRA-PLAT-423)
- Is client-side batching feasible for the top 10 customers causing needles? Ask solutions-eng for client integration effort estimate.

Slack blurb (one-liner to paste)
"Quick vignette: short dense bursts (needles) cost more per-query despite similar token totals because slot packing and context-switch overheads drive tail latency and utilization loss — see sketch in platform/needle-valley. Actionable: try small opportunistic aggregation + steer to tiny models for micro-requests."

Appendix: micro-run logs (trimmed)
- Needle run sample (excerpt)
  - t=0.002s: session 1001 queued -> dispatched (slot 1) -> gen 7 tokens -> complete 0.018s
  - t=0.006s: session 1002 queued -> wait 0.040s due to slot busy -> p90 spike
  - tail: several sessions waited >350ms for slot preemption finish (KV flush)
- Valley run sample (excerpt)
  - even spacing avoided preemption collisions; few waits >80ms

Notes to self
- Validate with 2 more models (smaller and larger) and with/without quantization VA to ensure kernel behavior not dominating.
- Add a simple chart generator that prints these ASCII sparklines automatically from bench outputs.

References / next steps
- Attach to internal playbook PR: github.com/redwood-inference/platform-playbooks/pull/214
- Follow-up ticket: JIRA-PLAT-423 (data sampling), JIRA-PLAT-424 (client batching feasibility)

-- Aisha (draft)
